source.title: Investigating the Impact of Model Complexity in Large Language Models
source.authors: Jing Luo; Huiyuan Wang; Wei-Ran Huang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, but the supplied text contains figure captions rather than the plotted data for Figures 1–3.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests model-size risk using HMM-based theory and a synthetic head-tuning Transformer experiment, with a different method from the original empirical studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own model-size risk theory and synthetic experiment. Cited results from Nakkiran et al. and other work are not recorded as rows. Figure 2 is described as showing a rightward shift in the threshold as the sample count grows; that does not establish that more data raises test error near the threshold.
record.test_reason: The study derives its own risk curves for ridgeless least-squares head tuning on HMM-generated data. It also runs a synthetic head-tuning experiment on a frozen random Transformer. Both bear directly on whether risk peaks at interpolation and falls again past it. Because this is a new setting (multivariate, HMM-dependent data) rather than a new method on the original question, T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely right. The authors conclude that head tuning under HMM modelling shows double descent with a degenerate initial descent: risk rises toward p/n=1 and falls beyond it, and the frozen-Transformer simulation matches this. They add that the optimum lies at p<n (the 'sweet spot' is at size zero), so training data should greatly exceed model size. They also show that larger n shifts the peak rightward.
record.recipe_differences: Uses HMM-based theoretical multivariate regression and a synthetic head-tuned Transformer experiment, rather than the original studies' empirical sweeps over deep-network size, training time, and sample size.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that increasing the training sample count shifts the interpolation threshold toward larger model size. It also varies noise variance in Figure 1, but the supplied text does not state the resulting differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the training sample count n shifts the interpolation peak toward larger model size p (Figure 2, Remark in Section 3.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The model-wise interpolation peak moves with sample size, located at p≈n.

record.problems: The analysis is restricted to a linear representation and a trained linear head under an HMM-based synthetic setup; the Transformer experiment also uses HMM-generated data and only 20 test samples per dataset. The text provides no numerical empirical curve values or uncertainty estimates for the simulation, and the supplied figures are not rendered.
record.rows_left_out: No separate Figure 2 row: its stated result is a rightward shift of the interpolation threshold as sample count grows, not a reported increase in test error from adding data. No epoch-wise result is reported.

untested.parts: No size sweep of fully trained deep networks or real pretrained LLMs. Only a frozen random 1-layer Transformer with a linear head is tested.
Entirely untested; there is no sweep over training time or epochs.
Figure 2 varies n, but the paper never reports test error rising with more samples at fixed model size. It reports only the rightward shift of the peak.
Only linear regression under HMM data and a random-feature Transformer are covered; no broader range of model classes.
Entirely untested; no single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
Multiple peaks are not tested. Ridge appears only as a proof device, so there is no result on whether the peak vanishes under optimally tuned regularization.
Entirely untested; complexity is not re-counted with an effective parameter number.

missing.what: Statement that prediction error/test loss is minimized when model size p is smaller than training sample count n (theory and simulation). This bears on whether the second descent improves over the underparameterized regime.

record.verdict_notes: The theory is a near-direct multivariate extension of Hastie et al. (2022) to dependent HMM data. Theorem 2 excludes the immediate neighbourhood of the threshold. The paper's own formulas imply a sample-wise non-monotonicity: at fixed p>n, raising n toward p raises risk. The paper does not state this, so V3 is left untested. The simulation has only 20 test samples, no error bars, and no plotted values in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test model-size sweeps in real pretrained LLMs or across broad model families.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
Does not report that increasing sample size raises test error near the interpolation threshold.
Theoretical and experimental settings are limited to the paper's HMM-based regression setup and synthetic head-tuned Transformer; it does not test a broad range of model classes.
Does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The paper varies noise variance in a figure, but the supplied text does not expose the plotted values or state the noise effect. It does not test multiple peaks or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Does not recalculate complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that produces an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.value: Tr(Σϵ) γ/(1−γ); the text says risk increases as γ approaches 1.
rows.note: Risk rises in the underparameterized regime rather than initially falling as V1 specifies.
rows.check: This is a linear least-squares model, not a deep network, so it does not bear on V1. 'Reversed' is wrong: risk rising to a peak at γ→1 is the peak the double-descent curve predicts. The missing classical dip is a scope qualifier, not an opposite effect. The text says the underparameterized risk is variance only and scales with Tr(Σϵ), so the row also bears on V6's noise-driven peak.

The decline is stated in the text; no numbers are given. The authors also say minimum risk lies at p<n, so the second descent does not beat the underparameterized optimum.

Results are figure-only, with ntest=20 and no uncertainty.
